Course 11

Sleep and the mind

Why we sleep, what happens in each stage, how it affects mood and which habits really help.

Lesson 3. Sleep and mood

1 · Lesson

The link between sleep and mental health runs both ways. Poor sleep worsens mood, anxiety and the ability to handle stress; and almost every mental health problem disrupts sleep.

Insomnia is persistent difficulty falling or staying asleep, or waking too early, with consequences during the day. It is common and, when it becomes chronic, it is usually kept going by habits and thoughts that feed it: lying awake in bed for long periods, worrying about not sleeping, or making up for it with long naps.

People with insomnia are at higher risk of developing depression, and treating insomnia can improve mood. That is why, in primary care, asking about sleep is a simple way to open a conversation about how someone is doing.

2 · Example

A night of short sleep makes the amygdala, involved in emotional responses, react more strongly to negative images, with weaker control from frontal areas. It is one reason everything seems worse after a bad night.

3 · Activity

Think about your last bad night. Write down what worried you the next day and how much it affected you, from 1 to 10. A few days later, after sleeping well, rate the same thing again. Has it changed?
